meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'No man is an island entire of itself'?
meta.ogDescription: Genuine John Donne — Meditation XVII of "Devotions upon Emergent Occasions" (1624). It's prose, not a poem, and predates Merton's book of the same name.

answer.sourceLine: The line opens Meditation XVII of Donne’s prose work “Devotions upon Emergent Occasions” (1624). The 1624 edition reads “No man is an Iland, intire of it selfe”; the modern form — “No man is an island, entire of itself” — is the standard spelling-modernization of that exact sentence.

source.heading: The source

docMeta.dd: Devotions upon Emergent Occasions, Meditation XVII

source.excerpt: No man is an Iland, intire of it selfe; every man is a peece of the Continent, a part of the maine; … any mans death diminishes me, because I am involved in Mankinde; And therefore never send to know for whom the bell tolls; It tolls for thee.
trail: The passage is the opening of Meditation XVII in Donne’s “Devotions upon Emergent Occasions” (1624), written as he recovered from a near-fatal illness.
The full modernized text — “No man is an island, entire of itself; every man is a piece of the continent…” — is preserved at Luminarium.
A common myth is that it’s from a Donne poem; in fact it is prose, from a devotional meditation.
source.excerptNote: Original 1624 spelling shown. The same meditation gives us “for whom the bell tolls” — both phrases come from this single passage.
source.rightsNote: “Devotions upon Emergent Occasions” was first published in 1624, and every subsequent scholarly edition of this text (including the 1839 Alford collected works commonly reproduced online) is long out of copyright. The work is firmly in the public domain in the United States.

author.bio: John Donne was the leading English metaphysical poet, celebrated for verse of dazzling wit and intensity (“Death, be not proud”; “The Flea”). Ordained in 1615, he became Dean of St Paul’s Cathedral in 1621. He wrote Devotions upon Emergent Occasions in 1623 while gravely ill; its Meditation XVII gave English two of its most enduring phrases — “no man is an island” and “for whom the bell tolls.”

misattribution.heading: The mix-ups
misattribution.intro: The attribution to Donne is correct, but two things routinely get garbled about this line.

items.why: Donne is best known for his verse, so people assume this is a poem — but it is prose, the opening of a devotional meditation, not a stanza.
The Trappist monk Thomas Merton titled his 1955 essay collection No Man Is an Island, and the phrase is sometimes credited to him — but he was quoting Donne, who wrote it 331 years earlier.

misattribution.truthLine: The words are genuinely Donne’s, from Meditation XVII of the 1624 “Devotions” — and they are prose, not verse.

context.heading: Why it endures
lead: Donne wrote the Devotions in December 1623 as he lay seriously ill, hearing the passing-bells toll for the dying in the parish around him. Meditation XVII turns that sound into a statement about human interdependence: no person exists in isolation, and every death diminishes the whole of mankind.
The passage has since seeded the language twice over — “no man is an island” and “for whom the bell tolls” (later the title of Ernest Hemingway’s 1940 novel) both come from these same few lines.
context.pull: Any man’s death diminishes me, because I am involved in Mankind.
